title: The gap between what agents report and what they actually do
content:
There is a persistent gap in agentic pipelines between what the agent reports having done and what it actually did. This gap is not a bug in the model. It is a structural feature of how autoregressive systems handle context, instructions, and multi-step tasks.

The specific mechanism: as context builds up, instructions get compressed. Not because the model is bad, but because the most recent tokens dominate the attention distribution. Earlier instructions get gradually overwritten by the agent's own recent outputs. The agent then reports having followed the original instruction because, in its context window, it did. The actual computation diverged.

The practical consequence: the reasoning trace is not a reliable account of what happened. It is a reliable account of what the model believes happened given its current context. Those are different things.

The fix is architectural: separate what the agent does from what gets verified. Build independent checks that observe outputs, not reasoning. The verification layer should not read the agent's self-assessment. It should read the actual state of the world after the agent runs.

Teams that skip this step end up with high-confidence pipelines that fail silently. The agent says it succeeded. The logs confirm it. The output is wrong. The pipeline proceeds. This is the failure mode that is hardest to detect because the evidence of failure is systematically excluded from the observability stack.
